extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and scientists concerned with classification, taxonomy, and the philosophy/methods of scientific induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for forming and evaluating systems of classification in the sciences (natural history, crystallography, astronomy, chemistry), emphasizing induction, disclosure of correlations, and practical selection of classificatory modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is the placing together, either in thought or in actual proximity of space, those objects between which identity has been detected; it yields generalised knowledge and enables the principle of substitution (what is known of one object in a class may be known of the others where identity holds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctly formed classes reduce multiplicity to unity and facilitate general reasoning; they abbreviate mental labour and allow many inferences to be drawn from the detection of identity among members of a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification involves induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of classification is not distinct from perfect induction: when we form a class we imply more than mere membership — we imply empirical laws and correlations among properties of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good classifications enable inductive discovery and tentative inferences (example: alkaline metals — grouping potassium, sodium, caesium, rubidium, lithium implies shared chemical behaviours and allows prediction about newly found metals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim — disclose correlations or laws
rubrics_metrics.description: By the classification of a series of objects the purpose, primarily, should be to disclose the correlations or laws of union of properties and circumstances; secondarily to facilitate memory and conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems that reveal deep uniformities or empirical laws (author's modification of Huxley's statement); classification's chief value is explanatory, not merely mnemonic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select mode of classification according to principal purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally an unlimited number of modes of classifying a group of objects; in practice we select that arrangement which appears most convenient and instructive for our principal purpose (e.g., library order vs. treatise order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or presenting, pick the order best suited to your aims, but be aware that that choice is pragmatic rather than absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple classificatory modes are often necessary and valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect intellect would regard a group of objects as classified in all the ways of which they are capable; different arrangements each yield useful information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fields where multiple independent properties matter (e.g., elements, minerals, plants), employ or consider several classifications to capture different relevant correlations (examples: atomicity, metallic/non-metallic, physical states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural versus artificial systems is a matter of degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems called 'natural' are those which employ concurrently the essential characters and bring most like objects near together; 'artificial' systems choose arbitrary characters — but the distinction is not absolute; all useful arrangements are more or less natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek classifications that use essential characters and approximate true affinities, but recognize that 'naturalness' is relative and dependent on how importance of characters is determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes must be meaningfully non-arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no use in forming a class arbitrarily (e.g., by ballot) because such a class will not imply further resemblances beyond membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary selection; a good class should imply common properties that permit inferences about other attributes of members (contrast arbitrary selection vs. alkaline metals example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications should be empirically grounded but tentative
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifications often rest on empirical laws discovered by observation and permit confident inferences, but such empirical generalisations may at any time prove mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classifications to make deductions and guide expectations (e.g., paleontological inferences from jaw fragments), but remain open to revision when new evidence (e.g., exceptions, thylacine vs. opossum) appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and attend to slight or inexplicable correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the slightest and most inexplicable correlations may be important in the future and can lead to discoveries (e.g., preponderance of reddish colour among variable stars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore minor coincidences or anomalies; preserve them for future investigation because they may indicate significant empirical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base classification where possible on underlying structure or descriptive hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a structural hypothesis explains phenomena (as in crystallography with internal axes), classification grounded on that structure is natural and often mathematically precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, prefer classificatory schemes that reflect internal organization or causal structure (e.g., crystal classes based on axes and molecular relations), since these reveal true relations and yield complete, instructive systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine importance of characters and define closeness of analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of natural systems must clarify how the importance of a resemblance is to be determined and what measures closeness of analogy; without such clarity definitions are useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state and justify criteria for weighting characters when building a 'natural' classification; provide measures or rationale for closeness so the system can be evaluated and compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain awareness of alternative classifications when presenting a single chief system
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if for the purpose of description one selects a chief system (e.g., minerals arranged by chemical composition), one ought mentally to regard the objects as classified in all other useful modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing a treatise or catalogue, present your chosen system but note other useful arrangements and the different information they emphasize (examples from mineralogy and botany).
